articles.title: Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute launches to address challenges facing our brain health
articles.description: Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute launches to address challenges facing our brain health Abby Munson Fri, 09/25/2026 - 10:42 The Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute brings together researchers from across the University to work alongside patients, carers, practitioners, policymakers and innovators to help understand and support individuals experiencing cognitive and emotional difficulties at every stage of life. Our brain health is at increasing risk from everything from digital lifestyles, diet, physical inactivity, acute or chronic illnesses, climate change, conflicts to social cohesion. Yet we don’t fully understand why or how these factors affect our cognitive and emotional well-being, and why each of us responds differently. As a result, current treatments for conditions affecting the brain and mind are often ineffective. The Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute, announced today ahead of its official launch in in April 2027, brings together diverse expertise to tackle these challenges. Researchers will have access to cutting-edge on-site neuroimaging and brain stimulation techniques, supported by technical expertise, advanced methods advice and scientific computing. The facilities can also be used by members of the wider research community. The institute will train tomorrow’s translational cognitive neuroscientists through its postgraduate research degrees, taught programmes, shorter courses and training workshops. This autumn, it will welcome its first cohorts of postgraduate students and researchers to the new MPhil in NeuroAI and Intelligent Systems and established MPhil in Cognitive Neurosciences . Both programmes provide exceptional foundation training in cutting-edge research topics and techniques. Professor Deborah Prentice, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, said: “The Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute will unite world-class research, facilities and the lived experiences of patients and partners. By unlocking the mysteries of brain and mind health, it aims to transform how we understand and support individuals experiencing cognitive and emotional difficulties at every stage of life.” Founded by the Departments of Psychology and Psychiatry as a cross-School hub for cognitive neuroscience with real-world relevance, the institute will build on the expertise established at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit. The Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute will galvanise cognitive neuroscience activity across the University via a weekly headline lecture series and diverse academic events. Scheduled events during the Institute’s first term include a showcase for postdoctoral researchers, an EDI and wellbeing day, and research culture workshop. The Institute will also strengthen involvement of the general public and special interest groups in brain and mind research via participatory, outreach and engagement activities. Carly Hood, a postgraduate student, said: “It’s great to see the Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute encouraging an open, collaborative culture, where creative individuals with different expertise can work together towards shared questions around mental health and human cognition. I look forward to the opportunity to working with and learning from people who bring fresh perspectives from a wide variety of diverse disciplines.” For more information about CMBI, and to find out how you can get involved, visit www.cmbi.cam.ac.uk The Cambridge Mind and Brain Institute will unite world-class research, facilities and the lived experiences of patients and partners. articles.title: Stay motivated and healthy this school year
articles.description: With courseload ramping up, academic and personal stress has settled into most people's lives. Here are my best tips for staying disciplined, motivated, organized and, most importantly, happy and healthy this fall. 1) 3-2-1 method I often find that the transition phase between tasks is the hardest to overcome. If I'm in my bed and scrolling on my phone, the task of getting up and locking in seems daunting. To combat this, I use the 3-2-1 method: in my head, I'll count down from 3 and get up when I reach 1. This gives my mind something to do and distracts me while I get ready to start my task. I notice that after I begin, the work seems less stressful and I can truly concentrate. 2) Notes app I don't know if it's just me, but I hate using planners. The task of having to lug around a book with me at all times is hard for me to stick to. Instead, I utilize the Notes app on my phone that I sync with my computer. Being able to jot everything down at a moment's notice and organize when I get home is more convenient and effective. 3) Take breaks When you're on hour two or three of studying, your mind can lose focus easily. I find that taking a break is vastly beneficial. Different ways to take breaks: - Pomodoro method: 25 minutes of working followed by a five minute break, and repeat. You can find custom timers online, especially on Youtube, that can help set the aesthetic appeal of your study session (rain ambience is my favorite). - Switching between tasks: If you have more than one type of work to do, it's best to take breaks from one type of work to do another type of work. It gives different parts of your brain time to rest. For example, yesterday I had terms to memorize for psychology and a long article to read for my film class. I divided my time equally between the two, spending 25 minutes on one and then 25 minutes on another. I felt more refreshed and productive, and I was able to focus for longer. - Go for a walk: The most underrated form of taking a break. Sitting for long periods of time can slow your circulation and make you tired. Get your blood flowing on a walk, and you'll feel refreshed and ready to approach your work again with a fresh perspective. 4) Don't overload There are so many cool organizations here, and I would love if I could join them all. At the Student Involvement Fair, I definitely felt some serious decision fatigue. However, overloading yourself with work can be detrimental, and you'll often find that putting your energy into two or three things you're super passionate about is better than joining as many clubs as possible and doing half-hearted work. 5) Optimal sleep Contrary to popular belief, not all hours of the night are worth the same. Research from the Cleveland Health Clinic suggests that the best hours to be asleep are from 10pm to 2am, as that is when your body's natural circadian rhythm maximizes deep sleep and melatonin production. When given a choice, it's always better to prioritize sleep in this timeframe, even if that means having to wake up at an earlier time the next day to get work done. 6) Mindset is everything While hard work is valuable, nothing is more important than your physical and mental health. Working too hard can cause a multitude of issues, and no one gets an award for suffering. Instead of overloading yourself, constructing a schedule that maximizes your own personal health and happiness is the most important of all. Make sure to do the things you like, whether that be having fun with friends or setting aside time to do your favorite hobbies. With good time management, you can thrive. On campus, there are a multitude of resources to help if you are struggling. Go to this link to seek professional support if you are feeling down. It is never embarrassing to ask for help! Stay safe, Blue Jays, and have a good semester!

articles.title: Stanford Engineers Teach Spacecraft to "Dream" Their Way to the Space Station
articles.description: Docking with the ISS may seem simple. However, actually doing so is a showcase in how difficult orbital mechanics can be. It’s equivalent to traveling down a highway at 28,000 km/hr and parallel parking into an open garage on a multi-billion dollar laboratory traveling at the same speed. If you try to accelerate forward you actually drift up, and there’s no air friction to naturally slow you down. Oh, and if you hit the lab, everyone onboard both your craft and the station dies, and the resultant debris field could both wipe out dozens of satellites and even people on the ground. No pressure, obviously. For decades, aerospace engineers have been docking successfully using hard coded physics equations and human pilots to correct them. But now, a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at Stanford, is taking a shot at building an AI to perform a series of “mental simulations” that could fundamentally change how future spacecraft interact with each other.

articles.title: Engineering the Substation Exit for Reliability, Capacity, and Expansion
articles.description: This white paper gives distribution engineers and utility teams a practical overview of the substation exit, the short and high-consequence section where station capacity divides into individual feeders. It explains how covered, spacer-supported overhead construction can reduce common contact-driven faults while leaving room for future circuits. What you will learn about: Why a fault near the substation exposes more customers than one farther along the feeder, and why the first spans out of the station carry so much reliability weight. How covered conductors and spacer-cable systems differ from bare overhead conductors, and why covered conductor is not treated as touch-safe insulation. Which engineering factors shape a sound exit design, including conductor rating, protection coordination, grounding, and structural loading. How overhead spacer cable compares with conventional bare overhead and underground shielded cable across footprint, reliability, and lifecycle cost. How to move a project from concept to commissioning using staged design gates and a clear performance specification. Download this free whitepaper now!
